newsitem.title: SPAIN: Grieving Spain unites against ETA and its allies.
newsitem.headline: Grieving Spain unites against ETA and its allies.

text.p: Spaniards steeped in grief and anger lashed out on Sunday with unprecedented fury and unanimity at ETA Basque separatist rebels after they killed a kidnapped politician despite mass public protests.
Rage and indignation poured out from even the most diehard nationalist corners of the northern Basque region at what was seen as a senseless killing and a sign of ETA's increasing desperation.

"After this vile assassination, ETA is more isolated than ever," Basque political leaders said in a statement after an urgent meeting on Sunday. "If they were not loved yesterday, they are despised today."
The shock turned to violence in some parts and clashes broke out between ETA sympathisers and opponents.

ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) abducted 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco on Thursday afternoon. The guerrillas killed him two days later after the government refused a demand to transfer about 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the Basque region by 4 p.m. on Saturday.
The Basque leaders, many of whom are sympathetic to the separatist movement, said they would tolerate no further contact with ETA or its political wing Herri Batasuna.

"The universe of Herri Batasuna is an accomplice to this act. The blood of this victim weighs on them," nationalist Basque leader Jose Antonio Ardanza said. "It is time for them to be denounced publicly."

Popular resentment against ETA, which has killed some 800 people in a nearly 30-year campaign for an independent Basque state, has grown steadily in the last decade but Herri Batasuna (HB) consistently gains about 15 percent of the Basque vote.

Central government and regional politicians joined all but the most radical media on Sunday in calling for the complete isolation of Herri Batasuna and a stop to its voter support as the only way to end Basque separatist violence.

"ETA exists because HB exists. Avoid them like the plague...look the other way when they pass on the street," the leading newspaper El Pais said in a front-page editorial on Sunday. "We cannot be tolerant of those who are intolerant, nor leave apologists for terrorism unpunished."
ETA attacks have provoked nationwide outrage and massive street protests in the past.

A 1987 bomb in a Barcelona hypermarket that killed 21 shoppers and the gunning down of a well-respected judge in central Madrid last February brought Spaniards to the streets by the hundreds of thousands.

But it was the poignant image of ETA's death threat hanging over the head of such an ordinary person -- Blanco was a councillor in a small Basque town with plans to marry -- that cut to the heart of Spanish society and caused such a furore.
"Miguel could be any one of us, that's why it hurts," one protester in the Basque separatist stronghold Bilbao said on Saturday.
"It shows they can play with the life of anyone."
Blanco's kidnap was also a flashpoint because only days earlier the country had been celebrating the release of two other ETA hostages.

Spaniards, particularly those in the troubled Basque region, took to the streets in historic numbers on Saturday with a half a million people led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar marching through Bilbao to demand Blanco's freedom.
Former ETA members and others within the universe of the separatist guerrilla movement published pleas for his release.

The sliver of hope opened by those messages combined with the overwhelming response of the Spanish society made the sense of impotence and outrage that much deeper when Blanco was found shot and near death shortly after ETA's 4 p.m. deadline.
The pain and shock that the separatists had cut down the life of someone many Spaniards could identify with was plainly written on people's faces across the nation.
Even the sister of an ETA prisoner could not believe the group had carried out their threat.
"We don't understand what ETA is trying to do, we are completely overwhelmed and destroyed," she said in a teary-eyed interview on state television.

Despite the public opposition, ETA has always managed to attract underprivileged youths from the fringes of society, although they are often more interested in the excuse to lash out at the system than nationalist issues.
Basque guerrillas started fighting for independence under the dictatorship of the late General Francisco Franco, when the region was subject to intense repression and their cause had popular support.
